content: An introduction to the basic functions of the SigMesh protocol and the responsibilities of its protocol layers.
title: SigMesh Network Fundamentals

content: 1. Feature Overview SigMesh is a mesh network application-layer protocol built on top of Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE). It reuses the BLE link layer directly without any modification. A general mesh network needs to solve the following problems: Mesh network management: How do nodes join or leave the network? What is the maximum number of nodes? Are low-power nodes supported? Message delivery between nodes: One-to-one communication (unicast) and one-to-many communication (groupcast)? Message latency and how to find the best path? What is the maximum distance over which a mesh network can reliably deliver messages? How is reliable delivery guaranteed? How large can an application payload be in a single packet? How are segmentation, reassembly, and reliability handled? How does the mesh network ensure security? The SigMesh standard is based on a flooding mechanism. It uses the BLE link-layer advertising channels to deliver messages. Any node within radio range can receive a message and relay it to extend the delivery range. Future revisions of the specification may add routing and define enhancements for routing-based mesh networks. Network storm: As the number of nodes grows, unrestricted relaying can saturate the network bandwidth, preventing normal messages from being delivered and eventually causing a network storm that paralyses the mesh network. Message relay: SigMesh currently provides two mechanisms to limit unlimited relaying in a flooding network: a message cache and a maximum relay count (TTL). Message cache: Every message is added to a cache list to prevent a device from relaying messages it has already received. When a message arrives, it is checked against the list and ignored if it is already present. Otherwise, it is added to the cache so that future copies can be ignored. To keep the list from growing indefinitely, the number of cached messages is limited by the implementation. TTL: Every message contains a time-to-live (TTL) value that limits how many times it may be relayed. Each time a device receives and relays a message (up to 126 times), the TTL is decremented by one. Communication support: Some existing BLE devices may not support mesh messages over advertising. To allow these devices to join a mesh network without hardware or software upgrades, the mesh network provides a GATT bearer for devices such as phones and tablets. Low power: Control messages for low-power nodes are handled through a friendship with a node that supports the Friend feature. Node provisioning: The Provisioner adds and removes nodes from the mesh network. Provisioning can use either the advertising bearer or the GATT bearer. In theory, any node can act as a Provisioner.
title: SigMesh Network Fundamentals

content: 2. Node Features In addition to basic message sending and receiving, nodes in a SigMesh network can optionally provide several extra features. Friend: Caches messages that a low-power node has not yet processed so that the low-power node can retrieve them after waking up. A node that enables the Friend feature and establishes a friendship with a low-power node becomes a Friend node. Relay: Receives and forwards mesh messages over the advertising bearer to extend the network range. Proxy: Receives and forwards mesh messages between the GATT bearer and the advertising bearer. Low Power: A battery-powered node that does not stay awake continuously. When receiving messages, it can significantly reduce power consumption by working with a node that supports the Friend feature.
title: SigMesh Network Fundamentals

content: 3. Network Topology The figure shows three Relay nodes: Q, R, and S. The three nodes that support the Friend feature are N, O, and P. However, N does not have any friendships; therefore only O and P are Friend nodes. There are five Low Power nodes: I, J, K, L, and M. Nodes I, J, and K have P as their friend, while L and M have O as their friend. Node T is connected to the mesh network only through a GATT bearer; therefore S must relay all messages to and from T. For example, if a message is to be sent from T to L, T sends it to node S over the GATT bearer. Node S retransmits the message over the advertising bearer. Nodes H, R, N, and O are within radio range of S and therefore receive the message. Node O, as L’s friend, stores the message. If the message is segmented, O responds with an acknowledgment at the lower transport layer. Later, L polls O for new messages, and O forwards the message originally sent by T to L.
title: SigMesh Network Fundamentals

content: 4. Key Concepts To describe the functions and mechanisms of a SigMesh network more precisely, the Mesh standard defines several concepts: states, messages, bindings, elements, addressing, models, publish-subscribe, mesh keys, and associations. States: A state is a value representing a condition of an element. Bound states: A state-binding mechanism inside a node or between nodes. For example, the switch state of a switch node can be bound to the on/off state of a light node. Messages: Nodes in a mesh network communicate by sending messages. For a given state, a server defines a set of messages that clients can use to get or change the state. A message consists of an opcode and related parameters. Standard messages use a 2-byte opcode, special-purpose messages use a 1-byte opcode, and vendor-specific messages use a 3-byte opcode. The transport layer determines the maximum message size and may use segmentation and reassembly (SAR). To maximize performance and avoid SAR overhead, the design goal is to fit a message into a single segment. When the transport layer does not segment a message, the application payload can contain up to 11 bytes, including the opcode. The SAR mechanism provided by the transport layer supports up to 32 segments and a maximum message size of 384 bytes. SAR does not introduce extra space overhead: a 10-byte message fits in one segment, while a 20-byte message uses two segments. Messages are also classified as acknowledged (ACK) and unacknowledged messages. Elements: An element is an addressable entity within a node. Every node has at least one element. The number of elements cannot change after the node is provisioned and remains fixed for the lifetime of the node. If a firmware upgrade changes the number of elements, the node must be re-provisioned. Models: A model defines the basic functionality of a node. For example, a light may have a brightness model and a color model, and a node may contain multiple models. The standard defines three types of models: Server model, Client model, and Control model. Addresses: Unicast address: A unique address assigned to each element, ranging from 0x0001 to 0x7FFF, for a total of 32,767 addresses. Virtual address: Ranges from 0x8000 to 0xBFFF, for a total of 16,384 addresses. Group address: 0xFF00 to 0xFFFF are reserved for fixed purposes, while 0xC000 to 0xFEFF are available for user-defined group addresses.
title: SigMesh Network Fundamentals

content: 5. Protocol Layers
title: SigMesh Network Fundamentals

content: 5.1 Model layer Defines the set of capabilities that nodes with different roles may use in a mesh network. Each model contains a set of states and messages and is identified by a Model ID. See the official Mesh Model Specification for details.
title: SigMesh Network Fundamentals

content: 5.2 Foundation Model layer Similar to the Model layer, this layer defines models related to network configuration and management.
title: SigMesh Network Fundamentals

content: 5.3 Access layer The access layer defines how higher-layer applications use the upper transport layer. It defines the application data format and controls application data encryption and decryption performed by the upper transport layer.
title: SigMesh Network Fundamentals

content: 5.4 Upper transport layer Messages from the access layer are encrypted and authenticated with the AppKey. This allows the upper transport layer to verify messages received from the network layer. Transport control messages generated inside the upper transport layer are encrypted and authenticated only at the network layer.
title: SigMesh Network Fundamentals

content: 5.5 Lower transport layer When necessary, the lower transport layer handles PDU segmentation and reassembly.
title: SigMesh Network Fundamentals

content: 5.6 Network layer The network layer encrypts and decrypts data with the NetKey. It also forwards node messages and implements the network message cache.
title: SigMesh Network Fundamentals

content: An introduction to the basic characteristics, version evolution, protocol architecture, and learning path of Bluetooth, a guide to the world of Bluetooth technology.
title: Getting Started with Bluetooth Protocols

content: 1. A Brief History of Bluetooth Bluetooth is a wireless communication standard that lets fixed and mobile devices exchange data over short distances and form a personal area network (PAN). It uses short-wavelength UHF radio waves in the 2.4–2.485 GHz ISM band. Ericsson, a telecommunications company, developed the technology in 1994. The original goal was to create a wireless replacement for RS-232 data cables. Bluetooth can connect multiple devices and overcome synchronization issues. The Bluetooth SIG (Special Interest Group) maintains the standard. It has more than 30,000 member companies across telecommunications, computing, networking, and consumer electronics. The IEEE once standardized Bluetooth as IEEE 802.15.1, but that standard is no longer maintained. Technology types: Bluetooth has two technology types: Basic Rate/Enhanced Data Rate (BR/EDR) and Low Energy (LE). BR/EDR uses a point-to-point topology for one-to-one device communication. LE supports point-to-point (one-to-one), broadcast (one-to-many), and mesh (many-to-many) topologies. The Bluetooth SIG owns the Bluetooth trademark, develops the specifications, certifies manufacturers, and licenses the use of Bluetooth technology and trademarks. It does not design, manufacture, or sell Bluetooth devices itself.
title: Getting Started with Bluetooth Protocols

content: 1.2 Bluetooth 2.x + EDR Bluetooth 2.0 + EDR introduced the “non-hopping narrowband channel.” Because it does not require an acknowledgement exchange with every device, this channel can broadcast various Bluetooth service profiles to a large number of Bluetooth devices at once. The acknowledgement exchange currently takes about one second. Unencrypted information such as real-time public transport timetables, basic traffic conditions, and advanced traffic directions can be sent to devices at high speed. It also supports higher connection speeds and multiple speed levels. On July 26, 2007, the Bluetooth SIG adopted Bluetooth Core Specification 2.1 + EDR. It is fully backward compatible with version 1.2 and adds Sniff power-saving, which extends the contact interval between an adapter and a device to 0.5 seconds and can save a noticeable amount of power. It also adds Secure Simple Pairing (SSP), which improves the pairing experience and increases security.
title: Getting Started with Bluetooth Protocols

content: 1.3 Bluetooth 3.0 + HS On April 21, 2009, the Bluetooth SIG released Bluetooth Core Specification 3.0 (3.0 + HS), which introduced a new alternate RF technology. Bluetooth 3.0 + HS increased data transfer rates, and with 802.11 PAL it can reach a maximum speed of 24 Mbps, eight times the speed of Bluetooth 2.0. It also introduced enhanced power control, significantly reducing idle power consumption.
title: Getting Started with Bluetooth Protocols

content: 1.4 Bluetooth 4.x Bluetooth 4.0 differs from the mainstream Bluetooth 2.x + EDR and the not-yet-widespread Bluetooth 3.0 + HS in its protocol composition. Bluetooth 4.0 is the only comprehensive protocol specification in Bluetooth’s history and defines three modes: Bluetooth Low Energy, Classic Bluetooth, and High Speed Bluetooth. High Speed Bluetooth: focused on data exchange and transfer. Classic Bluetooth: focused on information exchange and device connections. Bluetooth Low Energy: focused on connections for devices that do not need much bandwidth. Its predecessor was Wibree, developed by Nokia as an extremely low-power mobile wireless communication technology. After the SIG adopted and standardized it, it was renamed Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE). These three specifications can be combined to enable a wider range of applications. Bluetooth 4.0 also extends the transmission range to more than 100 meters in low-energy mode. Bluetooth 4.0 defines Single mode and Dual mode. Single mode can communicate only with Bluetooth 4.0 and is not backward compatible with 3.0/2.1/2.0. Dual mode is backward compatible and can communicate with both Bluetooth 4.0 and 3.0/2.1/2.0 devices. Frequency hopping: Bluetooth uses adaptive frequency hopping across all specification versions to minimize interference with other 2.4 GHz ISM-band wireless technologies. At the end of 2013, the Bluetooth SIG released Bluetooth 4.1, aiming to make Bluetooth Smart a core driver of the Internet of Things (IoT). In December 2014, the Bluetooth SIG released Bluetooth 4.2.
title: Getting Started with Bluetooth Protocols

content: 1.5 Bluetooth 5.x Bluetooth 5.0 was released in June 2016. It offers four times the range and twice the speed of Bluetooth 4.2 LE (up to 24 Mbps). Bluetooth 5.0 also supports indoor positioning and navigation (combined with Wi-Fi, it can achieve indoor positioning accuracy of less than one meter) and allows devices to receive beacon data without pairing, such as advertisements, beacons, and location information, with an eightfold increase in throughput. It also includes many low-level optimizations for IoT. In January 2019, the Bluetooth SIG released Bluetooth 5.1. In January 2020, the Bluetooth SIG released Bluetooth 5.2.
title: Getting Started with Bluetooth Protocols

content: 1.6 Summary Bluetooth 4.0 is not the same as BLE. BLE is only a subset of Bluetooth 4.0; Bluetooth 4.0 is a comprehensive protocol specification. Since Bluetooth 4.0, the technology has been divided into Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) and Classic Bluetooth (BR/EDR). Most chips on the market support only BLE, while some support both (dual-mode Bluetooth chips). Three functional configurations of Bluetooth chips:
title: Getting Started with Bluetooth Protocols

content: 2. The Bluetooth Protocol Stack The Bluetooth protocol stack consists of three major parts: Host + optional HCI + Controller. Single-chip solutions do not use HCI. Host: The host consists of the core protocols (L2CAP, SDP, SMP, ATT) and core specifications (GAP, GATT). Controller: This part is divided into Bluetooth Low Energy (Vol 6: Low Energy Controller) and Classic Bluetooth (Vol 2: BR/EDR Controller). HCI: Defines the interface standard between the host and the controller (Vol 4: Host Controller Interface). It can use UART, USB, or other transports. In the figure above, red indicates required BR/EDR Classic Bluetooth components, green indicates required LE components, and blue indicates shared components. Classic Bluetooth can also implement the green features. The HCI interface depends on the chip architecture and is optional. The figure does not show the physical-layer differences between the two technologies; this is outside chip design and can be ignored for now. GAP (Generic Access Profile): Defines the basic functions of all Bluetooth devices, including device discovery, connection, pairing, and bonding procedures; the four Bluetooth device roles; the format of advertising and scan response packets; and common Bluetooth parameters such as device address, name, pairing keys, and appearance, which identify whether a device is a phone or a computer. It also specifies the basic requirements for a BLE device, including which layers it must contain and how they work together. Defines four Bluetooth device roles: broadcaster, observer, peripheral, and central. A broadcaster must be able to send advertising packets but may have no receiver, such as a beacon sensor. An observer must be able to receive packets from broadcasters but may have no transmitter; in practice, such devices are rare. A peripheral uses connectable advertising events to establish a link-layer connection and becomes a slave after connecting; it must be able to both receive and transmit. A central receives a connectable advertising packet from a peripheral and can initiate a connection; after connecting, it becomes a master and must be able to both receive and transmit. Defines common Bluetooth parameters: Bluetooth device address, device name, pairing key, and appearance value (used to identify whether a device is a phone or a computer). For more details, see in the Core_v4.2.pdf the Part C: Generic Access Profile chapter, which compares the GAP specifications for Classic Bluetooth and BLE. ATT (Attribute Protocol): Defines a set of rules for accessing data on a peer device. It is the foundation of GATT and a cornerstone of BLE. It defines the attribute message format and message types used by the host. Requests: Sent by a client to a server and require a Response. (C->S, acknowledged request) Responses: Sent by a server in response to a client Request. Commands: Sent by a client to a server and do not require a response. Notifications: Sent by a server to a client without a response. Indications: Similar to Notifications, but the client must send Confirmations to acknowledge receipt. Confirmations: Paired with Indications. GATT (Generic Attribute Profile): Built on top of ATT, GATT defines attribute types and how they are used. It standardizes the data content of attributes and uses the concept of groups to classify and manage attributes. Without GATT, a BLE protocol stack can still run, but interoperability becomes a problem. L2CAP (Logical Link Control and Adaptation Protocol): Hides many controller transport details from higher layers, simplifies higher-layer protocol development, and provides segmentation and reassembly (SAR), flow control, retransmission, and message integrity checks. SMP (Security Manager Protocol): Defines security operations such as pairing, authentication, and encryption for Bluetooth devices. LLCP/LL (Link Layer Control): For BLE, see in the Core_v4.2.pdf the Part B: Link Layer Specification chapter. PHY (Physical Layer): BLE
title: Getting Started with Bluetooth Protocols

content: 3. Learning Path This section gives a basic learning path for BLE. It may not suit everyone; feel free to discuss it in the comments. Core idea: learn by asking questions, such as “How do BLE devices establish a connection?” and “What is the connection keep-alive mechanism in BLE?” Build a basic understanding of the protocol stack, its components, and the terminology, and form an overall picture. Analyze packet captures from real projects and connect theory with observed behavior for each procedure, such as BLE advertising and connection establishment. If possible, get a development board with matching tutorial code that you can run directly. Port and study a protocol stack implementation. Zephyr is recommended.
title: Getting Started with Bluetooth Protocols
